explain.say: Concrete is about ten times weaker when stretched, so on its own the bottom would crack and the beam would snap. Steel bars, called rebar, are placed near the bottom to carry that tension.

explain.say: The bars sit a few centimetres inside, under a layer called the cover, which protects them from rust and fire. Steel and concrete expand by almost the same amount when heated, so they stay bonded together.

faq.q: Why do we put steel in concrete?
faq.a: Concrete is strong when squeezed but cracks easily when stretched. Steel bars are cast inside where the concrete will be stretched and carry that tension, making reinforced concrete strong both ways.

faq.q: Which part of a concrete beam is squeezed?
faq.a: In a simple beam resting on two supports, the top is squeezed, in compression, and the bottom is stretched, in tension. In a cantilever it is the other way round.
asks: Where is compression in a beam?

faq.a: It is the line through a bending beam where there is no squeezing or stretching. Material near it does little work, which is why I-beams put most of their material far from it.
asks: What is the middle of a beam doing?

faq.q: Why is rebar buried inside the concrete?
faq.a: The concrete cover, usually a few centimetres thick, shields the steel from water and air so it does not rust, and protects it from fire, which would weaken it.

faq.q: Where does the rebar go in a concrete beam?
faq.a: Mostly near the bottom of a beam between supports, where it is stretched, and near the top over supports or in cantilevers, where the stretching moves to the top. Extra loops called links help resist shear.
asks: Why is rebar at the bottom of a beam?

facts: Steel and concrete expand by almost the same amount with temperature, which lets them work together without cracking apart.
Joseph Monier, a French gardener, patented iron-reinforced concrete plant tubs in 1867 and later extended the idea to building.
